extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, regulatory analysts, agency rule drafters, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and measuring how and why federal agencies reuse regulatory text (regulatory diffusion), including network-based leadership/follower metrics and the incentives and channels that produce text reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership measured by number of agencies that have copied from an agency
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative way to conceptualize leadership within a network is by looking at the number of agencies that have copied from another agency. These nodes have the most edges connected to other agencies; that is, how many spokes are in the most active hubs within the network?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize leadership by counting distinct borrowing agencies that use language from a given agency (see Table 3). Use a minimum-paragraph threshold (the paper uses a minimum of five paragraphs borrowed) to reduce outliers. This metric highlights agencies whose language is broadly imitated across the system (example leaders: DOJ, IMLS-related entities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader agencies by number of borrowing agencies (minimum-of-five-paragraphs threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top leader agencies according to an alternate metric for agencies with a minimum of five copied paragraphs (Table 3). The numbers represent the number of agencies that have borrowed from the agency listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a paragraph-count threshold (e.g., >=5 paragraphs) to distinguish systematic borrowing from one-off or outlier copying. Use the resulting counts to rank leaders; interpret with attention to agency subject-matter breadth and cross-cutting statutory roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follower score: number of unique paragraphs an agency borrowed
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'follower score' measured by the number of unique paragraphs that an agency borrowed (Table 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute for each agency the total count of unique paragraphs copied from other agencies to identify top followers (example: DHS highest follower score). Use this score to infer incentives such as recent creation, jurisdictional breadth, and resource constraints that drive borrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted lender–borrower pair frequency (directional weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify strongest lender–borrower relationships between individual agencies and compute the weighted frequency of each unique agency pair, taking direction of reuse into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a weighting scheme that accounts for uncertainty about source agency and treats A→B differently from B→A. Use weighted frequencies to surface prominent dyadic relationships (e.g., Treasury→DOT; Treasury→DHS) and to interpret jurisdictional overlap and historical ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of borrowed text by executive vs independent agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure rates at which executive and independent agencies borrow paragraphs from executive or independent lenders (Table 6 shows percentages for executive/independent lender and borrower combinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute share of borrowed paragraphs originating from executive vs independent agencies and compare to baseline shares of paragraphs promulgated by each group to detect systematic biases. Interpret elevated within-group borrowing (e.g., independent agencies borrowing more from other independent agencies) as trust/expertise dynamics rather than simple prevalence effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command-and-control (political principal direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Text reuse can result from direction from a political principal—Congress or the President—who sometimes requires agencies to issue regulations that mimic those of another or creates overlapping functions that encourage sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify statutory or executive directives that require similarity or coordination (example: Securities and Exchange Act directing substantially similar regs; Exec. Orders like EO 12250 requiring Attorney General coordination). Treat mandated coordination or statutory cross-application (e.g., FOIA, Privacy Act) as structural drivers of diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-group and lobbyist pressure (model regulations/templates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups and lobbyists supply model legislation and model regulations to agencies; private actors also propose regulatory text via petitions and comments, encouraging agencies to adopt prepackaged language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for external templates (model laws/regulations, industry-developed model rules) and formal petitions/comments proposing text (e.g., NCLA petitions, NAIC model laws). Consider undisclosed or informal channels by which stakeholders deliver ready-to-use drafts as a low-cost influence mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning (emulation of 'successful' rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies learn from others and emulate rules perceived as successful—those upheld in court, well-interpreted, or that foster compliance. Where success is hard to observe, drafters use proxies (e.g., rules not abandoned over time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat prior litigation survival, interpretive stability, compliance outcomes, or longevity as signals of success. Lawyers favor language that has survived litigation, so agencies may adopt such language to reduce legal risk. Learning induces standardization and 'mix and match' of proven provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource costs and time pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Resource constraints—deadlines, budget/staff limits, 'midnight rules'—make text reuse attractive because drafting from scratch is costly and requires multi-disciplinary coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect higher borrowing when agencies face statutory deadlines, political time pressure, or limited staffing/budgets. Consider measuring correlation between resource indicators (budget, staffing) and reuse rates. Recognize that reuse can also lower barriers to amendment ('deossify' rulemaking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory consistency and coordination as a driver
rubrics_metrics.description: Text reuse promotes regulatory consistency across agencies and helps new language integrate into an existing complex CFR system; copying can avoid unintended inconsistencies and reduce industry compliance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine instances where harmonization is explicitly sought (statutes requiring consult/coordination, agency comments urging harmonization like SEC/CFTC example). Use evidence of stakeholder investment in prior rules as impetus for harmonizing new rules to existing ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of diffusion (formal and informal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts diffuse through many channels: simple search of CFR, informal observation, formal consultation requirements, bilateral MOUs, presidential policy councils, regulatory review (OIRA), interagency template projects (e.g., DOJ FOIA template), and coordinating offices like OGIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map and document both low-friction channels (CFR search, imitation) and institutional channels (statutory consultations, OIRA review, RMOs, policy councils, interagency template efforts). Evaluate effectiveness case-by-case (e.g., mixed success of DOJ FOIA template across agencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB/OIRA and RMOs as diffusion influencers (model rules and resource levers)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB—including OIRA and its resource-management offices (RMOs)—shapes rulemaking by reviewing significant rules (evaluating policy and cost–benefit) and using budgetary levers; components like the Office of Federal Procurement Policy promulgate model rules that others emulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing diffusion, account for OMB's political/analytical review and RMOs' budgetary influence. Identify model rules issued by OMB components as likely seed texts for cross-agency copying (example: procurement model rules adopted widely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency drafting culture and stakeholder relationship (cooperative vs litigious)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's relationship with its regulated entities (cooperative vs adversarial) and internal drafting practices can affect the detail and attractiveness of its regulations as models (example: Treasury/OCC's cooperative approach yields detailed rules worthy of emulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether agencies with cooperative engagement produce more granular, practitioner-informed provisions that other agencies are likely to borrow. Consider role of embedded examiners or close supervision (OCC) as producing template-ready language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional breadth, agency history, and subcomponent autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's jurisdictional breadth and institutional history (e.g., DHS's combining of many components) makes it more likely to borrow from many sources; subcomponents within agencies may be drafting leaders or followers, explaining mixed leader/follower status for parent agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret high follower or leader scores in light of agency mergers, transferred components (Coast Guard from DOT to DHS), and internally heterogeneous offices. Analyze subcomponent-level activity where possible rather than only parent-agency aggregates.
